import tensorflow as tf
from tensorflow.keras.layers import Layer, Dense, Input, Dropout, LayerNormalization, BatchNormalization
from tensorflow.keras.models import Model
from tensorflow.keras import regularizers
from tensorflow.keras.optimizers import Nadam
from tensorflow.keras.callbacks import EarlyStopping, ModelCheckpoint, LearningRateScheduler
from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
import numpy as np
from tensorly.decomposition import tucker, tensor_train

# Sampling Function
def random_sampling(data, sample_size):
    return data[np.random.choice(data.shape[0], sample_size, replace=False)]

# Approximation Function using Polynomial Approximation
def polynomial_approximation(inputs, degree):
    return np.poly1d(np.polyfit(np.arange(len(inputs)), inputs, degree))(np.arange(len(inputs)))

# Dimensionality Reduction using PCA
def apply_pca(data, n_components):
    pca = PCA(n_components=n_components)
    return pca.fit_transform(data)

# Define the Stochastic Cellular Automaton Layer
class SCALayer(Layer):
    def __init__(self, grid_size, iterations, **kwargs):
        super(SCALayer, self).__init__(**kwargs)
        self.grid_size = grid_size
        self.iterations = iterations

    def build(self, input_shape):
        self.prob = self.add_weight(shape=(self.grid_size, self.grid_size),
                                    initializer='random_normal',
                                    trainable=True)

    def call(self, inputs):
        grid = inputs
        for _ in range(self.iterations):
            random_grid = tf.random.uniform(shape=(self.grid_size, self.grid_size))
            mask = tf.less(random_grid, self.prob)
            grid = tf.where(mask, grid + 1, grid - 1)
        return grid

# Define the Partition Function Layer for Statistical Mechanics
class PartitionFunctionLayer(Layer):
    def __init__(self, **kwargs):
        super(PartitionFunctionLayer, self).__init__(**kwargs)

    def call(self, inputs):
        energy_states = inputs
        partition_function = tf.reduce_sum(tf.exp(-energy_states))
        return partition_function

# Define the Stochastic Matrix Layer for Markov Chain Analysis
class StochasticMatrixLayer(Layer):
    def __init__(self, state_size, **kwargs):
        super(StochasticMatrixLayer, self).__init__(**kwargs)
        self.state_size = state_size

    def build(self, input_shape):
        self.transition_matrix = self.add_weight(shape=(self.state_size, self.state_size),
                                                 initializer='random_normal',
                                                 trainable=True)

    def call(self, inputs):
        state_probabilities = tf.nn.softmax(tf.matmul(inputs, self.transition_matrix))
        return state_probabilities

# Define the Correlation Function Layer
class CorrelationFunctionLayer(Layer):
    def __init__(self, **kwargs):
        super(CorrelationFunctionLayer, self).__init__(**kwargs)

    def call(self, inputs):
        mean = tf.reduce_mean(inputs)
        centered_inputs = inputs - mean
        correlation = tf.reduce_mean(centered_inputs * tf.roll(centered_inputs, shift=1, axis=1))
        return correlation

# Define the Tucker Decomposition Layer
class TuckerDecompositionLayer(Layer):
    def __init__(self, ranks, **kwargs):
        super(TuckerDecompositionLayer, self).__init__(**kwargs)
        self.ranks = ranks

    def call(self, inputs):
        core, factors = tucker(inputs.numpy(), ranks=self.ranks)
        return tf.convert_to_tensor(core)

# Define the Tensor Train Decomposition Layer
class TensorTrainDecompositionLayer(Layer):
    def __init__(self, ranks, **kwargs):
        super(TensorTrainDecompositionLayer, self).__init__(**kwargs)
        self.ranks = ranks

    def call(self, inputs):
        tt_cores = tensor_train(inputs.numpy(), rank=self.ranks)
        return tf.convert_to_tensor(tt_cores)

# Define the Functor Layer
class FunctorLayer(Layer):
    def __init__(self, functor, **kwargs):
        super(FunctorLayer, self).__init__(**kwargs)
        self.functor = functor

    def call(self, inputs):
        return self.functor(inputs)

# Define the neural network architecture
def create_sca_network(input_shape, grid_size, iterations, state_size, output_units, l2_reg, tucker_ranks, tt_ranks):
    inputs = Input(shape=input_shape)
    x = SCALayer(grid_size, iterations)(inputs)
    partition_function = PartitionFunctionLayer()(x)
    stochastic_matrix_output = StochasticMatrixLayer(state_size)(partition_function)
    correlation_function_output = CorrelationFunctionLayer()(stochastic_matrix_output)
    tucker_output = TuckerDecompositionLayer(tucker_ranks)(correlation_function_output)
    tt_output = TensorTrainDecompositionLayer(tt_ranks)(tucker_output)
    x = Dense(128, activation='swish', kernel_regularizer=regularizers.l2(l2_reg))(tt_output)
    x = BatchNormalization()(x)
    x = Dropout(0.3)(x)
    x = Dense(64, activation='swish', kernel_regularizer=regularizers.l2(l2_reg))(x)
    x = BatchNormalization()(x)
    x = Dropout(0.3)(x)
    outputs = Dense(output_units, activation='softmax')(x)
    model = Model(inputs, outputs)
    return model

# Example usage

iterations = 5

        self.functor = functor

    def call(self, inputs):
        return self.functor(inputs)

# Define the neural network architecture
def create_sca_network(input_shape, grid_size, iterations, state_size, output_units, l2_reg, tucker_ranks, tt_ranks, activation_function):
    inputs = Input(shape=input_shape)
    x = SCALayer(grid_size, iterations)(inputs)
    partition_function = PartitionFunctionLayer()(x)
    stochastic_matrix_output = StochasticMatrixLayer(state_size)(partition_function)
    correlation_function_output = CorrelationFunctionLayer()(stochastic_matrix_output)
    tucker_output = TuckerDecompositionLayer(tucker_ranks)(correlation_function_output)
    tt_output = TensorTrainDecompositionLayer(tt_ranks)(tucker_output)
    
    x = Dense(128, activation=activation_function, kernel_regularizer=regularizers.l2(l2_reg))(tt_output)
    x = BatchNormalization()(x)
    x = Dropout(0.3)(x)
    x = Dense(64, activation=activation_function, kernel_regularizer=regularizers.l2(l2_reg))(x)
    x = BatchNormalization()(x)
    x = Dropout(0.3)(x)
    outputs = Dense(output_units, activation='softmax')(x)
    
    model = Model(inputs, outputs)
    return model

# Example usage
input_shape = (10, 10)
grid_size = 10
iterations = 5
state_size = 10
output_units = 10
l2_reg = 0.01
tucker_ranks = [5, 5, 5]
tt_ranks = [5, 5, 5]
sample_size = 50  # Sample size for random sampling

# Generate example data

labels = tf.keras.utils.to_categorical(np.random.randint(0, 10, 100), 10)

# Apply random sampling
inputs = random_sampling(inputs, sample_size)
labels = labels[:sample_size]

# Normalize the input data
scaler = StandardScaler()
inputs = scaler.fit_transform(inputs.reshape(-1, input_shape[0]*input_shape[1])).reshape(-1, input_shape[0], input_shape[1])

# Apply PCA for dimensionality reduction
inputs = apply_pca(inputs.reshape(inputs.shape[0], -1), n_components=20).reshape(-1, 10, 2)

# Augment the data
inputs = augment_data(inputs)

# Define the model with LeakyReLU activation function as an example
activation_function = LeakyReLU()

# Compile and train the model with different optimization algorithms
optimizers = {'nadam': Nadam(), 'adam': Adam(), 'rmsprop': RMSprop(), 'sgd': SGD(momentum=0.9)}

for opt_name, optimizer in optimizers.items():
    print(f"Training with optimizer: {opt_name}")
    model = create_sca_network(input_shape, grid_size, iterations, state_size, output_units, l2_reg, tucker_ranks, tt_ranks, activation_function)
    model.compile(optimizer=optimizer, loss='categorical_crossentropy', metrics=['accuracy'])
    
    # Define callbacks
    early_stopping = EarlyStopping(monitor='val_loss', patience=10, restore_best_weights=True)
    checkpoint = ModelCheckpoint(f'best_model_{opt_name}.h5', monitor='val_loss', save_best_only=True, mode='min')
    lr_schedule = LearningRateScheduler(lambda epoch: 1e-3 * 10 ** (epoch / 20))
    
    # Train the model
    model.fit(inputs, labels, epochs=50, callbacks=[early_stopping, checkpoint, lr_schedule], validation_split=0.2)
    
    # Evaluate the model
    model.evaluate(inputs, labels)

# Define the hyperparameters to tune
param_grid = {'iterations': [3, 5, 7], 'l2_reg': [0.001, 0.01, 0.1]}

# Perform grid search to find the best hyperparameters
grid = GridSearchCV(estimator=model, param_grid=param_grid, cv=3)
grid_result = grid.fit(inputs, labels)

# Print the best hyperparameters
print("Best: %f using %s" % (grid_result.best_score_, grid_result.best_params_))

# Train the model with the best hyperparameters
best_params = grid_result.best_params_
model = create_sca_network(input_shape, grid_size, best_params['iterations'], state_size, output_units, best_params['l2_reg'], tucker_ranks, tt_ranks, activation_function)
model.compile(optimizer=Nadam(), loss='categorical_crossentropy', metrics=['accuracy'])

# Define callbacks
early_stopping = EarlyStopping(monitor='val_loss', patience=10, restore_best_weights=True)
checkpoint = ModelCheckpoint('best_model.h5', monitor='val_loss', save_best_only=True, mode='min')
lr_schedule = LearningRateScheduler(lambda epoch: 1e-3 * 10 ** (epoch / 20))

# Train the model
model.fit(inputs, labels, epochs=50, callbacks=[early_stopping, checkpoint, lr_schedule], validation_split=0.2)

# Evaluate the model
model.evaluate(inputs, labels)

import sqlparse
from sqlparse.sql import IdentifierList, Identifier
from sqlparse.tokens import Keyword, DML

# Define a basic translation dictionary for SQL dialects
translation_dict = {
    'mysql': {
        'SERIAL PRIMARY KEY': 'AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY',
        'BOOLEAN': 'TINYINT(1)'
    },
    'postgresql': {
        'AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY': 'SERIAL PRIMARY KEY',
        'TINYINT(1)': 'BOOLEAN'
    }
}

def translate_query(query, target_dialect):
    """
    Translates a given SQL query to the target dialect.
    
    :param query: The SQL query to be translated
    :param target_dialect: The target SQL dialect ('mysql', 'postgresql')
    :return: Translated SQL query
    """
    parsed = sqlparse.parse(query)
    translated_query = []

    for stmt in parsed:
        for token in stmt.tokens:
            if token.ttype is Keyword or token.ttype is DML:
                # Translate SQL keywords and types
                token_value = token.value.upper()
                if token_value in translation_dict.get(target_dialect, {}):
                    translated_query.append(translation_dict[target_dialect][token_value])
                else:
                    translated_query.append(token.value)
            else:
                translated_query.append(token.value)
    
    return ' '.join(translated_query)

# Example usage
query = "CREATE TABLE test (id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY, is_active BOOLEAN);"
target_dialect = 'mysql'

translated_query = translate_query(query, target_dialect)
print(f"Original Query: {query}")
print(f"Translated Query: {translated_query}")
```

class UnifiedSQLAccess:
    def __init__(self):
        self.engines = {
            'mysql': create_engine('mysql+pymysql://user:password@host/dbname'),
            'postgresql': create_engine('postgresql://user:password@host/dbname')
        }
        
    def execute_query(self, query, target_dialect):

        with self.engines[target_dialect].connect() as conn:
            result = conn.execute(text(translated_query))
            return result.fetchall()

### Gaussian Processes (GPs)

**Mathematics:**

- **Gaussian Processes (GPs)** are non-parametric models used for regression and classification tasks. A GP defines a distribution over functions and provides a flexible way to model complex data patterns.
- The joint distribution of a set of random variables follows a multivariate Gaussian distribution:$$
f(x) \sim \mathcal{GP}(m(x), k(x, x'))
$$where $m(x)$ is the mean function (usually assumed to be zero) and $k(x, x')$ is the covariance function or kernel that measures the similarity between points $x$ and $x'$.
- For classification, GPs can be used with a logistic or probit link function to model the probability of class membership.

**Application:**

- **Gaussian Processes** are versatile and can model uncertainty in predictions, making them suitable for tasks where confidence intervals are crucial. They are particularly effective for small to medium-sized datasets due to their computational complexity.

### Advanced Alternatives for Classification

**1. Ensemble Methods:**

- **Random Forests and Gradient Boosting:**
  - **Mathematics:** These methods combine multiple weak learners (usually decision trees) to create a strong learner. Random forests use bagging and random feature selection, while gradient boosting builds trees sequentially to correct errors of the previous trees.
  - **Application:** These methods are robust and can handle high-dimensional data with complex interactions.

**2. Neural Networks:**

- **Deep Learning Models:**
  - **Mathematics:** Neural networks consist of multiple layers of interconnected nodes (neurons), where each layer applies a non-linear transformation to the input data. The learning process involves optimizing a loss function using techniques like backpropagation and gradient descent.
  - **Application:** Deep neural networks (DNNs) and convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are powerful for image and text classification tasks. Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and their variants (e.g., LSTM, GRU) are effective for sequence data.

**3. Probabilistic Graphical Models:**

- **Conditional Random Fields (CRFs):**
  - **Mathematics:** CRFs are used for structured prediction tasks where the output variables have interdependencies. They model the conditional probability of the output sequence given the input sequence.
  - **Application:** CRFs are widely used in natural language processing (NLP) for tasks like named entity recognition (NER) and part-of-speech (POS) tagging.

### Modular Formulas and Advanced Mathematics for AI

Leveraging modular formulas and advanced mathematics can significantly enhance the capabilities of machine learning models. Here are some ideas for integrating advanced mathematical concepts into AI systems:

**1. Tensor Decompositions:**

- **Application:** Use tensor decompositions (e.g., Tucker decomposition, CP decomposition) to model multi-dimensional data. This approach can be particularly useful for tasks like multi-way data analysis and multi-relational learning.

**2. Topological Data Analysis (TDA):**

- **Mathematics:** TDA uses tools from algebraic topology to study the shape of data. Persistent homology, a key concept in TDA, captures the topological features of data across multiple scales.
- **Application:** TDA can be used to extract robust features from data, which can then be fed into machine learning models for improved performance.

**3. Advanced Optimization Techniques:**

- **Stochastic Gradient Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (SGHMC):**
  - **Mathematics:** SGHMC combines stochastic gradient descent with Hamiltonian Monte Carlo to improve convergence and exploration of the parameter space.
  - **Application:** This technique can be used to optimize complex models with many parameters, providing better convergence properties and uncertainty estimates.

Here’s an example code snippet that demonstrates the use of Gaussian Processes for binary classification using the gpflow library in Python:

```
import numpy as np
import gpflow
from gpflow.ci_utils import ci_niter
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score

# Generate synthetic data
np.random.seed(42)
X = np.random.randn(100, 2)
Y = (np.sin(X[:, 0]) + np.cos(X[:, 1]) > 0).astype(int).reshape(-1, 1)

# Split data into training and testing sets
X_train, X_test, Y_train, Y_test = train_test_split(X, Y, test_size=0.2, random_state=42)

# Define a kernel
kernel = gpflow.kernels.Matern52()

# Create a Gaussian Process Classifier model
model = gpflow.models.VGP((X_train, Y_train), kernel=kernel, likelihood=gpflow.likelihoods.Bernoulli())

# Optimize the model
opt = gpflow.optimizers.Scipy()
opt.minimize(model.training_loss, model.trainable_variables, options=dict(maxiter=ci_niter(1000)))

# Make predictions
Y_pred = model.predict_y(X_test)[0].numpy().round()

# Evaluate the model
accuracy = accuracy_score(Y_test, Y_pred)
print(f'Accuracy: {accuracy:.2f}')
```

To go beyond traditional methods like linear regression, k-nearest neighbors, and support vector machines, we can explore more advanced techniques that address their drawbacks and provide more powerful solutions. Here are some advanced regression and classification algorithms along with their key features and benefits:

### Advanced Regression Algorithms

**1. Ridge and Lasso Regression:**

- **Ridge Regression (L2 regularization):** Adds a penalty equal to the sum of the squared coefficients to the loss function, reducing the model complexity and preventing overfitting.
- **Lasso Regression (L1 regularization):** Adds a penalty equal to the sum of the absolute values of the coefficients, which can shrink some coefficients to zero, effectively performing feature selection.
- **Elastic Net:** Combines both L1 and L2 regularization.

**2. Decision Trees and Ensemble Methods:**

- **Random Forests:**
  - **Description:** An ensemble method that builds multiple decision trees and merges their results to improve accuracy and reduce overfitting.
  - **Pros:** Handles large datasets well, robust to noise, and provides feature importance.
- **Gradient Boosting Machines (GBM):**
  - **Description:** Builds models sequentially, each new model correcting errors of the previous ones.
  - **Pros:** High accuracy, handles various types of data well, and can model complex relationships.

**3. Bayesian Regression:**

- **Description:** Incorporates prior distributions into the regression model to handle uncertainty and provide probabilistic predictions.
- **Pros:** Provides probability estimates and is robust to overfitting with appropriate priors.

**4. Gaussian Processes for Regression (GPR):**

- **Description:** Non-parametric method that defines a distribution over functions and uses observed data to make predictions.
- **Pros:** Provides uncertainty estimates, handles small to medium-sized datasets well, and can model complex, non-linear relationships.

### Advanced Classification Algorithms

**1. Ensemble Methods:**

- **Random Forests and Gradient Boosting Machines (GBM):** As mentioned in regression, these methods are also highly effective for classification tasks.
- **XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost:**
  - **Description:** Advanced implementations of gradient boosting that are optimized for speed and performance.
  - **Pros:** Handle large datasets well, robust to overfitting, and provide high accuracy.

**2. Neural Networks and Deep Learning:**

- **Feedforward Neural Networks (FNN):**
  - **Description:** Composed of multiple layers of neurons that can model complex non-linear relationships.
  - **Pros:** Highly flexible and can approximate any continuous function given enough data and computational resources.
- **Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN):**
  - **Description:** Specialized for grid-like data such as images.
  - **Pros:** Highly effective for image classification tasks.
- **Recurrent Neural Networks (RNN) and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM):**
  - **Description:** Designed for sequence data.
  - **Pros:** Effective for time-series and natural language processing tasks.

**3. Probabilistic Graphical Models:**

- **Bayesian Networks and Conditional Random Fields (CRFs):**
  - **Description:** Model conditional dependencies between variables.
  - **Pros:** Provide probability estimates and are effective for structured prediction tasks.

**4. Support Vector Machines with Probabilistic Outputs:**

- **Description:** SVMs can be extended to provide probabilistic outputs using methods like Platt scaling or by using probabilistic SVM variants.
- **Pros:** Maintains the strengths of SVMs while providing probability estimates.

**5. k-Nearest Neighbors Variants:**

- **Weighted k-NN:**
  - **Description:** Weights the contributions of neighbors based on their distance to the query point.
  - **Pros:** Provides more nuanced predictions compared to traditional k-NN.

### Practical Considerations

When choosing more advanced methods, consider the following:

- **Model Complexity and Interpretability:** While more complex models can provide higher accuracy, they may also be harder to interpret. Techniques like feature importance in Random Forests or SHAP values for neural networks can help interpret complex models.
- **Computational Resources:** Advanced methods like deep learning require significant computational resources. Ensure you have the necessary hardware (e.g., GPUs) and infrastructure.
- **Hyperparameter Tuning:** Advanced models often have many hyperparameters. Use techniques like grid search, random search, or Bayesian optimization to find optimal hyperparameter settings.
- **Scalability:** Ensure the chosen method can handle the size and complexity of your dataset. Ensemble methods and neural networks are generally scalable to large datasets.

### Example: Gradient Boosting with XGBoost for Classification

Advanced regression and classification methods can significantly improve performance and robustness over traditional techniques like linear regression, k-nearest neighbors, and support vector machines. By leveraging ensemble methods, neural networks, probabilistic models, and other advanced techniques, you can build more powerful and versatile machine learning models.

    - These decompositions reduce the computational complexity and improve the model’s ability to capture higher-order interactions within the data.

4.  **Modular Design:**

    - The network architecture is designed to be modular, allowing easy experimentation with different tensor operations and decompositions.
    - This flexibility makes it easier to adapt the network to various types of data and tasks.

By integrating these enhancements, the Cantor Set neural network becomes more powerful, capable of capturing complex patterns, and robust against issues like vanishing gradients and information loss.

import torch

from tensorly.decomposition import tucker, tensor_train
import tensorly as tl

tl.set_backend('pytorch')

# Cantor Set Layer with Controlled Depth and Removal Pattern
class CantorSetLayer(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, input_dim, output_dim, depth=3, removal_pattern=[1, 1]):
        super(CantorSetLayer, self).__init__()
        self.input_dim = input_dim
        self.output_dim = output_dim
        self.depth = depth
        self.removal_pattern = removal_pattern
        self.weights = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(input_dim, output_dim))

    def cantor_mapping(self, x, depth):
        if depth == 0 or x.size(1) < sum(self.removal_pattern) + 1:
            return x @ self.weights
        else:
            sections = []
            start = 0
            while start < x.size(1):
                end = min(start + self.removal_pattern[0], x.size(1))
                if end < x.size(1):
                    sections.append(x[:, start:end])
                start = end + self.removal_pattern[1]
            mapped_sections = [self.cantor_mapping(section, depth-1) for section in sections]
            return torch.cat(mapped_sections, dim=1)

    def forward(self, x):
        return self.cantor_mapping(x, self.depth)

# Stacked CantorSetLayers

    def __init__(self, input_dim, hidden_dim, num_layers, depth=3, removal_pattern=[1, 1]):
        super(StackedCantorSetLayers, self).__init__()
        self.layers = nn.ModuleList([CantorSetLayer(input_dim if i == 0 else hidden_dim, hidden_dim, depth, removal_pattern) for i in range(num_layers)])

    def forward(self, x):
        for layer in self.layers:
            x = layer(x)
        return x

# Tensor Operations and Modular Formulas

        return x @ x.T
    elif operation == 'elementwise':

    elif operation == 'hadamard':

    elif operation == 'kronecker':
        return torch.kron(x, x)
    elif operation == 'concat':
        return torch.cat([x, x], dim=1)
    else:
        raise ValueError(f"Unsupported tensor operation: {operation}")

# Tucker Decomposition
def tucker_decomposition(x, ranks):
    core, factors = tucker(x, ranks=ranks)
    return tl.tenalg.multi_mode_dot(core, factors)

# TensorTrain Decomposition
def tensor_train_decomposition(x, ranks):
    tt_cores = tensor_train(x, rank=ranks)
    return tl.tt_to_tensor(tt_cores)

# Hierarchical Decompositions
class HierarchicalDecompositions(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, input_dim, tucker_ranks, tt_ranks):
        super(HierarchicalDecompositions, self).__init__()
        self.tucker_ranks = tucker_ranks
        self.tt_ranks = tt_ranks

    def forward(self, x):
        core, factors = tucker(x, ranks=self.tucker_ranks)
        coarse_tucker = tl.tenalg.multi_mode_dot(core, factors)
        tt_cores = tensor_train(coarse_tucker, rank=self.tt_ranks)
        fine_grained_tt = tl.tt_to_tensor(tt_cores)
        return fine_grained_tt

#### Modular Formula Integration

#### Tensor Encoding

Python



```
import torch

class TensorBTreeNode:
    def __init__(self, t):
        self.t = t  # Minimum degree (defines the range for number of keys)
        self.keys = []  # List to store keys
        self.children = []  # List to store child pointers
        self.leaf = True  # True if node is leaf, false otherwise

    def insert_non_full(self, key):
        i = len(self.keys) - 1
        if self.leaf:
            self.keys.append(0)
            while i >= 0 and key < self.keys[i]:
                self.keys[i + 1] = self.keys[i]
                i -= 1
            self.keys[i + 1] = key
        else:
            while i >= 0 and key < self.keys[i]:
                i -= 1
            if len(self.children[i + 1].keys) == 2 * self.t - 1:
                self.split_child(i + 1, self.children[i + 1])
                if key > self.keys[i + 1]:
                    i += 1
            self.children[i + 1].insert_non_full(key)

    def split_child(self, i, y):
        z = TensorBTreeNode(y.t)
        z.leaf = y.leaf
        z.keys = y.keys[self.t:]
        y.keys = y.keys[:self.t - 1]
        if not y.leaf:
            z.children = y.children[self.t:]
            y.children = y.children[:self.t]
        self.children.insert(i + 1, z)
        self.keys.insert(i, y.keys.pop())

class TensorBTree:
    def __init__(self, t):
        self.root = TensorBTreeNode(t)
        self.t = t

    def insert(self, key):
        root = self.root
        if len(root.keys) == 2 * self.t - 1:
            new_root = TensorBTreeNode(self.t)
            new_root.children.append(self.root)
            new_root.leaf = False
            new_root.split_child(0, self.root)
            self.root = new_root
            self.root.insert_non_full(key)
        else:
            self.root.insert_non_full(key)

    def traverse(self):
        self._traverse(self.root)

    def _traverse(self, node):
        for i in range(len(node.keys)):
            if not node.leaf:
                self._traverse(node.children[i])
            print(node.keys[i], end=' ')
        if not node.leaf:
            self._traverse(node.children[-1])

    def search(self, k, x=None):
        if isinstance(x, TensorBTreeNode):
            i = 0
            while i < len(x.keys) and k > x.keys[i]:
                i += 1
            if i < len(x.keys) and k == x.keys[i]:
                return (x, i)
            elif x.leaf:
                return None
            else:
                return self.search(k, x.children[i])
        else:
            return self.search(k, self.root)

# Example usage
btree = TensorBTree(3)
for i in range(10):
    btree.insert(i)

btree.traverse()

class HybridDataStructure:
    def __init__(self, hash_table_size, btree_t, tensor_params):
        self.hash_table = TensorHashTable(hash_table_size)
        self.knowledge_graph = TensorKnowledgeGraph()
        self.btree = TensorBTree(btree_t)

    def add_graph_node(self, node_id, features):

    def add_graph_edge(self, node1, node2, relation):
        self.knowledge_graph.add_edge(node1, node2, relation)

    def get_graph_node_features(self, node_id):
        return self.knowledge_graph.get_node_features(node_id)

    def get_graph_adjacency_tensor(self):
        return self.knowledge_graph.get_adjacency_tensor()

    def insert_btree(self, key):
        self.btree.insert(key)

    def traverse_btree(self):
        self.btree.traverse()

    def search_btree(self, key):
        return self.btree.search(key)

    def modular_tensor_operations(self, x, operation='matmul'):

    def tucker_decomposition(self, x):
        return tucker_decomposition(x, self.tensor_params['tucker_ranks'])

    def tensor_train_decomposition(self, x):
        return tensor_train_decomposition(x, self.tensor_params['tt_ranks'])

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F
import numpy as np
from tensorly.decomposition import tucker, tensor_train
import tensorly as tl

tl.set_backend('pytorch')

# Cantor Set Layer with Controlled Depth and Removal Pattern
class CantorSetLayer(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, input_dim, output_dim, depth=3, removal_pattern=[1, 1]):
        super(CantorSetLayer, self).__init__()
        self.input_dim = input_dim
        self.output_dim = output_dim
        self.depth = depth
        self.removal_pattern = removal_pattern
        self.weights = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(input_dim, output_dim))

    def cantor_mapping(self, x, depth):
        if depth == 0 or x.size(1) < sum(self.removal_pattern) + 1:
            return x @ self.weights
        else:
            sections = []
            start = 0
            while start < x.size(1):
                end = min(start + self.removal_pattern[0], x.size(1))
                if end < x.size(1):
                    sections.append(x[:, start:end])
                start = end + self.removal_pattern[1]
            mapped_sections = [self.cantor_mapping(section, depth-1) for section in sections]
            return torch.cat(mapped_sections, dim=1)

    def forward(self, x):
        return self.cantor_mapping(x, self.depth)

# Stacked CantorSetLayers
class StackedCantorSetLayers(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, input_dim, hidden_dim, num_layers, depth=3, removal_pattern=[1, 1]):
        super(StackedCantorSetLayers, self).__init__()
        self.layers = nn.ModuleList([CantorSetLayer(input_dim if i == 0 else hidden_dim, hidden_dim, depth, removal_pattern) for i in range(num_layers)])

    def forward(self, x):
        for layer in self.layers:
            x = layer(x)
        return x

# Tensor Operations and Modular Formulas
def modular_tensor_operations(x, operation='matmul'):
    if operation == 'matmul':
        return x @ x.T
    elif operation == 'elementwise':
        return x * x
    elif operation == 'hadamard':
        return torch.mul(x, x)
    elif operation == 'kronecker':
        return torch.kron(x, x)
    elif operation == 'concat':
        return torch.cat([x, x], dim=1)
    else:
        raise ValueError(f"Unsupported tensor operation: {operation}")

# Tucker Decomposition
def tucker_decomposition(x, ranks):
    core, factors = tucker(x, ranks=ranks)
    return tl.tenalg.multi_mode_dot(core, factors)

# TensorTrain Decomposition
def tensor_train_decomposition(x, ranks):
    tt_cores = tensor_train(x, rank=ranks)
    return tl.tt_to_tensor(tt_cores)

# Hierarchical Decompositions
class HierarchicalDecompositions(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, input_dim, tucker_ranks, tt_ranks):
        super(HierarchicalDecompositions, self).__init__()
        self.tucker_ranks = tucker_ranks
        self.tt_ranks = tt_ranks

    def forward(self, x):
        core, factors = tucker(x, ranks=self.tucker_ranks)
        coarse_tucker = tl.tenalg.multi_mode_dot(core, factors)
        tt_cores = tensor_train(coarse_tucker, rank=self.tt_ranks)
        fine_grained_tt = tl.tt_to_tensor(tt_cores)
        return fine_grained_tt

# Fractal Neural Network with Enhanced Features
class FractalNN(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, input_dim, hidden_dim, output_dim, cantor_depth=3, tensor_operation='matmul', decomposition='tucker', tucker_ranks=(5, 5), tt_ranks=(3, 3)):
        super(FractalNN, self).__init__()
        self.stacked_cantor_layers = StackedCantorSetLayers(input_dim, hidden_dim, num_layers=3, depth=cantor_depth, removal_pattern=[1, 1])
        self.hidden_layer1 = nn.Linear(hidden_dim, hidden_dim)
        self.hidden_layer2 = nn.Linear(hidden_dim, hidden_dim)
        self.output_layer = nn.Linear(hidden_dim, output_dim)
        self.dropout = nn.Dropout(0.5)
        self.tensor_operation = tensor_operation
        self.decomposition = decomposition
        self.tucker_ranks = tucker_ranks
        self.tt_ranks = tt_ranks
        self.hierarchical_decompositions = HierarchicalDecompositions(hidden_dim, tucker_ranks, tt_ranks)

    def forward(self, x):
        x = self.stacked_cantor_layers(x)
        x = modular_tensor_operations(x, self.tensor_operation)
        
        if self.decomposition == 'tucker':
            x = tucker_decomposition(x, ranks=self.tucker_ranks)
        elif self.decomposition == 'tensortrain':
            x = tensor_train_decomposition(x, ranks=self.tt_ranks)
        elif self.decomposition == 'hierarchical':
            x = self.hierarchical_decompositions(x)
        else:
            raise ValueError(f"Unsupported decomposition method: {self.decomposition}")

        # Adding decompositions within hidden layers
        x = F.relu(self.hidden_layer1(x))
        x = self.dropout(x)
        if self.decomposition == 'tucker':
            x = tucker_decomposition(x, ranks=self.tucker_ranks)
        elif self.decomposition == 'tensortrain':
            x = tensor_train_decomposition(x, ranks=self.tt_ranks)
        elif self.decomposition == 'hierarchical':
            x = self.hierarchical_decompositions(x)
        x = F.relu(self.hidden_layer2(x))
        x = self.output_layer(x)
        return x

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F
from torch.optim import Adam
from torch.optim.lr_scheduler import ReduceLROnPlateau

# Define Hebbian Learning mechanism (simplified version)
class HebbianLearning:
    def __init__(self, lr=0.01):
        self.lr = lr

    def update(self, weights, pre_activations, post_activations):
        delta_w = self.lr * torch.ger(post_activations, pre_activations)
        return weights + delta_w

# Define the Cantor Set Layer with self-modifying connections
class SelfModifyingCantorSetLayer(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, input_dim, output_dim, depth=3, removal_pattern=[1, 1], hebbian_lr=0.01):
        super(SelfModifyingCantorSetLayer, self).__init__()
        self.input_dim = input_dim
        self.output_dim = output_dim
        self.depth = depth
        self.removal_pattern = removal_pattern
        self.weights = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(input_dim, output_dim))
        self.hebbian = HebbianLearning(lr=hebbian_lr)

    def cantor_mapping(self, x, depth):
        if depth == 0 or x.size(1) < sum(self.removal_pattern) + 1:
            return x @ self.weights
        else:
            sections = []
            start = 0
            while start < x.size(1):
                end = min(start + self.removal_pattern[0], x.size(1))
                if end < x.size(1):
                    sections.append(x[:, start:end])
                start = end + self.removal_pattern[1]
            mapped_sections = [self.cantor_mapping(section, depth-1) for section in sections]
            return torch.cat(mapped_sections, dim=1)

    def forward(self, x):
        y = self.cantor_mapping(x, self.depth)
        self.weights.data = self.hebbian.update(self.weights.data, x.mean(dim=0), y.mean(dim=0))
        return y

# Define Meta-Learning component
class MetaLearner(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, network):
        super(MetaLearner, self).__init__()
        self.network = network

    def forward(self, x):
        # This is a placeholder for a more complex meta-learning strategy
        # Here, we simply forward the input through the network
        return self.network(x)

# Define Fractal Neural Network with Self-Modifying Architecture
class FractalFNN_SMA(nn.Module):

        self.cantor_layer = SelfModifyingCantorSetLayer(input_dim, hidden_dim, depth=cantor_depth, hebbian_lr=hebbian_lr)
